questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of the payback period?
options: The time taken for net cash inflows to cover the initial cost of an investment
The average annual return as a percentage of the investment
The total of discounted future cash flows minus the investment
The interest rate used to discount future cash flows
questions.why: Payback measures how soon the money comes back, which is a measure of risk and liquidity rather than profitability.
whyNot: That is the average rate of return.
That is net present value.
That is the discount rate.

questions.stem: An investment costs $400,000. Cumulative cash flow is negative $120,000 after year 2, and year 3 brings in $180,000. What is the payback period?
options: 2 years 8 months
2 years 4 months
3 years
2.67 years only
questions.why: (120 / 180) x 12 = 8 months, so payback is 2 years and 8 months.
whyNot: This appears to divide the wrong way: 180/120 rather than 120/180.
Payback occurs part way through year 3, not at the end of it.
The figure is right as a decimal, and the question expects years and months.

questions.stem: Total cash inflows over four years are $600,000 on an investment of $400,000. What is the average annual profit?
questions.why: Total net profit = 600,000 - 400,000 = $200,000. Average annual profit = 200,000 / 4 = $50,000.
whyNot: This divides total inflows by four without deducting the investment.
This appears to divide the net profit by two rather than four.
That is total net profit, not the annual average.

questions.stem: Average annual profit is $50,000 on an investment of $400,000. What is the ARR?
whyNot: This divides 400,000 by 50,000 incorrectly.
This divides the wrong way round.
ARR is a percentage, not a money amount.

questions.stem: Which method accounts for the time value of money?
options: Net present value
Payback period
Average rate of return
All three
questions.why: Only NPV discounts future cash flows to present value. Payback and ARR both ignore when the money arrives.
whyNot: Payback measures speed of return but does not discount.
ARR uses all cash flows and ignores their timing.
Only NPV does.

questions.stem: Discounted present values total $472,200 and the initial investment was $400,000. What is the NPV, and what should the business do?
options: Positive $72,200, so accept the project
Negative $72,200, so reject the project
Positive $872,200, so accept the project
The NPV cannot be calculated from this information
questions.why: NPV = 472,200 - 400,000 = +$72,200. A positive NPV means the project returns more than the discount rate used, so it should be accepted.
whyNot: 472,200 exceeds 400,000, so the NPV is positive.
This adds the investment instead of subtracting it.
Both figures needed are given.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of the payback method?
options: It ignores all cash flows after the payback point
It cannot be calculated without discount factors
It always gives a negative answer
It only works for very large investments
questions.why: A project paying back in three years then earning nothing looks better than one paying back in four years then earning for a decade. Payback also ignores the time value of money and gives no measure of profitability.
whyNot: It needs no discount factors.
It gives a time period.
It applies to investments of any size.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of the average rate of return?
options: It ignores the timing of the cash flows
It ignores cash flows after payback
It cannot be compared with interest rates
It requires discount factors
questions.why: A project earning most of its money in year one scores identically to one earning it in year four, which understates the value of early returns.
whyNot: ARR uses all the cash flows; that is payback's weakness.
Being a percentage is precisely what makes it comparable with interest rates.
It needs no discount factors.

questions.stem: Why is a project whose returns come late hurt most by discounting?
options: Later cash flows are multiplied by smaller discount factors, so they are worth much less today
Late cash flows are always smaller
Discounting only applies to the final year
Late returns are ignored entirely
questions.why: A factor of 0.68 in year 4 against 0.91 in year 1 means the same nominal amount is worth far less. That is exactly the weakness payback and ARR cannot capture.
whyNot: They may be any size; it is the factor applied to them that falls.
It applies to every future year.
They are included, at a reduced value.

questions.stem: What limitation applies to all three appraisal methods?
options: They all rely on forecast cash flows, which are estimates and often optimistic
They all require a computer
They all ignore the initial investment
They all give the same answer
questions.why: A precise NPV calculated from guesses is still a guess. All three are also purely financial and ignore staff, reputation, strategic fit and environmental impact.
whyNot: All three can be done by hand.
All three include it.
They frequently disagree, which is why businesses use more than one.

questions.stem: Why should a seasonal business weight payback heavily in its appraisal?
options: Loan repayments fall due in months with little revenue, so getting the money back quickly reduces risk
Payback is the most accurate method
Seasonal businesses cannot calculate NPV
Payback accounts for the time value of money
questions.why: Payback measures liquidity risk, which is the binding constraint when income arrives in a few months and obligations arrive in all twelve.
whyNot: It is the least sophisticated measure of profitability.
They can, and should.
It does not; only NPV does.
